question: Can a training-free, token-level gate based only on next-token distribution disagreement fuse a scientific specialist with a general reasoning model so that the resulting decoder is more accurate than either constituent without prohibitive inference overhead?

key_findings.claim: Divergence Decoding turns speculative draft-and-verify into an asymmetric capability router rather than a distribution-preserving accelerator.
key_findings.evidence: The specialist drafts blocks of ten tokens; the generalist evaluates all draft prefixes in one teacher-forced pass. At each position, a token is accepted from the specialist when top-support Jensen-Shannon divergence is below a threshold; above threshold the decoder samples one replacement from the generalist, discards the rest of the block, and returns to specialist drafting.

key_findings.claim: On the reported chemistry benchmarks, the fused policy usually improves over both components, but it does not dominate every task cell.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen-based ChemCoTBench, the method improves functional-group MAE from 0.21/0.24 to 0.17 and molecule-add accuracy from 45/40 to 70, but SMILES equivalence 0.85 is slightly below specialist 0.86. In the Llama pair it worsens ring MAE to 0.45 versus specialist 0.30, SMILES equivalence to 0.55 versus generalist 0.61, and substitution accuracy to 58 versus specialist 63. ChemBench likewise has isolated regressions such as technical chemistry 0.74 versus generalist 0.76.

key_findings.claim: The largest headline gains occur on GPQA-Diamond across three specialist-generalist pairs.
key_findings.evidence: Reported accuracies rise to 37.50% in chemistry versus 15.28% specialist and 23.61% generalist, 63.16% in biology versus 34.72% and 52.63%, and 70.93% in physics versus 26.74% and 61.62%. The paper does not provide confidence intervals, repeated sampling seeds, or significance tests for these finite benchmark subsets.

key_findings.claim: Top-10 JS is the strongest tested disagreement signal, but the ablation does not compare against the closest learned collaboration or logit-fusion systems.
key_findings.evidence: On ChemCoTBench, top-10 JS generally beats full cross-vocabulary JS, realized-token log-probability difference, and standard speculative sampling. Thresholds for each baseline are chosen to produce a small resampling fraction, but numerical ablation tables, router-based CITER/FusionRoute comparisons, simple logit ensembling, and oracle routing are absent.

key_findings.claim: Fallbacks are sparse and concentrated early, and they mostly inject connective reasoning language rather than scientific entities.
key_findings.evidence: Approximately 77% of resampling events occur in the first quarter of the generated reasoning trajectory. Most triggers combine high inter-model JS divergence with low generalist entropy, consistent with confident disagreement, and token categorization shows that injected tokens are predominantly general reasoning words with a smaller chemical/symbolic fraction.

key_findings.claim: The method's quality depends on benchmark-specific threshold calibration and decoding temperature.
key_findings.evidence: ChemCoTBench uses threshold 0.65 to inject about 3-5% of tokens, whereas ChemBench lowers the threshold to about 0.2 because the authors expect a larger reasoning contribution. Sensitivity tables over thresholds 0.56-0.66 and temperatures 0.2-1.2 show task-specific reversals rather than one uniformly optimal setting; no held-out calibration protocol is described.

key_findings.claim: Block verification keeps average latency close to a single model on the tested suite, but memory doubles and task-level latency varies widely.
key_findings.evidence: Overall ChemCoTBench generation time is 209.19 versus 200.16 for a single LLM, about 4.5% slower. Molecule editing is faster (169.43 versus 218.74), while molecule understanding is slower (233.04 versus 189.02); individual tasks range from 0.35x to 2.64x the single-model speed. Both large checkpoints must be loaded, and peak memory is not measured.

key_findings.claim: The theorem is a sufficient-condition result for one-step JS risk, not a demonstrated guarantee for sequence-level answer accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: The proof assumes the generalist is uniformly within epsilon_B of an unknown oracle distribution at every state, the specialist is strictly better on an in-domain subspace and at least epsilon_A wrong outside it, and the threshold perfectly separates those regions. It compares conditional risks under a common state expectation; it does not account for the different prefix/state distributions induced by each autoregressive policy or connect one-step JS risk to benchmark correctness.

method.core_idea: Use observable disagreement between a domain specialist and a robust generalist as a hard, training-free token router: default to the specialist, but let the generalist replace the first draft token whose predictive distribution diverges beyond a threshold.
method.mechanism: The specialist autoregressively drafts n=10 tokens and caches its next-token distributions. The generalist teacher-forces the same draft block to produce its distributions in parallel. Because model vocabularies/tokenizers can differ, text segments are aligned, probabilities are merged on aligned spans, and a union of each model's top-10 support is normalized before JS is computed. Low-JS draft tokens are retained; the first high-JS position is sampled from the generalist and invalidates the suffix. Both models use temperature 1.0, top-p 0.7, and top-k 10. Benchmark-specific thresholds regulate the intervention rate.
assumptions: The specialist and generalist have complementary rather than correlated errors.
Distributional disagreement is positively associated with specialist failure and not merely harmless tokenizer, calibration, or stylistic difference.
The generalist is a reliable fallback at high-disagreement states and does not overwrite crucial specialist knowledge.
Low disagreement implies the specialist is in its advantageous domain rather than both models sharing the same error.
Top-10, cross-tokenizer-aligned distributions preserve enough information for JS to approximate full predictive disagreement.
One generalist token can redirect the trajectory usefully before control returns to the specialist.
Thresholds calibrated separately for each benchmark do not leak test-set information or overfit task-specific behavior.
Comparing one-step oracle JS risks under a common state distribution is informative about the sequence-level policies despite autoregressive distribution shift.
The cost of loading and evaluating two full models is acceptable for the target scientific setting.

techniques.role: Uses a symmetric bounded distance between two next-token distributions as the routing score.
Preserves domain priors by invoking the generalist only at detected disagreement points.
Amortizes generalist evaluation across ten specialist draft positions rather than calling both models strictly token by token.
Replaces the earliest divergent token and discards the now-invalid suffix to maintain autoregressive consistency.
Merges probabilities over aligned text spans so heterogeneous model vocabularies can be compared.
Restricts divergence to the union of high-probability candidates to reduce noise and computation.
Locates where fallbacks occur along the chain and stratifies them by entropy and token type.
Tunes the threshold to control the fraction of generalist tokens injected for each task family.

evaluations.metric: Functional-group/ring MAE, Tanimoto-style scaffold and SMILES scores, and edit accuracy
evaluations.result: The router improves many cells, e.g. functional-group MAE 0.21/0.24 to 0.17 and add accuracy 45/40 to 70, but SMILES equivalence 0.85 trails the specialist's 0.86.
The router is best on several cells but loses ring MAE (0.45 versus 0.30 specialist), SMILES equivalence (0.55 versus 0.61 generalist), and substitution (58 versus 63 specialist).

evaluations.setting: ChemBench over nine chemistry subdomains for Qwen and Llama pairs
evaluations.result: The router is best in most subdomains; exceptions include Qwen materials science tied or below the specialist, Qwen technical chemistry below the generalist, and Llama technical chemistry 0.74 versus 0.76 generalist.
37.50%, 63.16%, and 70.93%, respectively, versus best constituent scores of 23.61%, 52.63%, and 61.62%.
evaluations.baseline: ChemDFM-R, TxGemma, or Raman-1.7B specialists and a common R1-Distill-Qwen-32B generalist

evaluations.result: Top-10 JS is reported best on most tasks and all divergence gates beat standard speculative sampling, but the figure supplies no uncertainty or direct learned-router comparison.
evaluations.baseline: Full cross-vocabulary JS, realized-token log-probability difference, and speculative sampling

evaluations.metric: Intervention position, generalist entropy, and token category
evaluations.result: About 77% of replacements occur in the first 25% of the trajectory and mostly involve confident generalist disagreement and general reasoning tokens.
evaluations.baseline: Later trajectory quarters and chemical/symbolic token categories

evaluations.setting: Threshold and temperature sweeps on ChemCoTBench
evaluations.result: Gains persist over several settings, but different thresholds/temperatures win different tasks and no single setting dominates the table.

evaluations.setting: End-to-end ChemCoTBench generation on four A800-80GB GPUs
evaluations.result: Overall 209.19 versus 200.16 seconds; molecule editing is faster but molecule understanding is slower, with large per-task variation.

limitations: Author-stated: benefit requires genuinely complementary errors; correlated failure or an unreliable generalist makes routing ineffective.
Author-stated: threshold, block size, temperature, and top-k support are extra hyperparameters that may need recalibration for every pair or domain.
Author-stated: both models must be loaded and queried, increasing memory even when block verification limits latency.
Author-stated: scientific outputs remain assistive and require domain-expert validation in safety-critical settings.
Reviewer-identified: headline claims that the method surpasses both constituents obscure several task-level regressions visible in Tables 1-2.
Reviewer-identified: no run seeds, sampling repeats, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported despite stochastic decoding and small benchmark subsets.
Reviewer-identified: benchmark-specific thresholds (about 0.65 versus 0.2) are motivated post hoc, with no held-out tuning split or calibration-selection procedure.

Reviewer-identified: the comparison omits the most direct collaboration baselines—Co-LLM, Expert Token Routing, CITER, FusionRoute, logit ensembling, and oracle/token classifiers—even though several are cited.
Reviewer-identified: the theorem's oracle closeness and hard domain-separation assumptions are not measured, and the proof ignores autoregressive occupancy-distribution shift.
Reviewer-identified: top-10 alignment is not the same JS divergence analyzed by the theorem, particularly for different tokenizers and long unaligned tails.
Reviewer-identified: evaluation is confined to three scientific benchmark families and does not test factuality, calibration, adversarial prompts, or real scientific workflows.
failure_modes: Both models can agree confidently on the same false continuation, yielding low JS and no intervention.
Models can disagree because of calibration, style, or tokenization rather than correctness, causing unnecessary or harmful fallback.
The generalist can replace a domain entity or symbol it understands less well, destroying a specialist-correct trajectory.
One injected token may redirect the prefix into a state where neither model's original reliability relation holds, creating cascading distribution shift.
Frequent early rejections discard most drafted blocks and make the two-model system substantially slower than single decoding.
Top-10 truncation can omit probability mass that distinguishes the models; cross-vocabulary segment merging can further distort divergence scale.
A threshold tuned to one dataset or intervention rate can over-route or under-route on a new domain, model scale, or decoding temperature.
If the specialist is much smaller or poorly calibrated, divergence becomes frequent and the system degenerates toward an expensive, interrupted generalist decoder.
A benchmark score can improve through sampling variance while scientific reasoning traces remain factually unsafe or chemically invalid.
reusable_insights: Model disagreement can serve as a training-free control signal when one model is designated a default and the other a conditional fallback.
The first high-impact token in a reasoning trajectory can matter more than averaging logits at every position; early intervention deserves separate analysis.
Blockwise teacher forcing can amortize a verifier over multiple draft states even when verification changes policy rather than preserving a target distribution.
A bounded symmetric distribution metric is more informative than the probability gap on only the realized token when routing between models.
Cross-tokenizer collaboration requires an explicit probability-alignment contract, and its approximation error should be evaluated as part of the router.
Control intervention frequency directly and report it alongside quality and latency; a threshold is also a compute-allocation knob.
Analyze fallback tokens by trajectory position, entropy, and semantic type to test whether the claimed division of labor actually occurs.
Evaluate every task cell against the better constituent, not only averages, because fusion can hide capability regressions.
open_questions: Can JS thresholds be calibrated on held-out data or online without labels and transferred across model pairs and domains?
How does the method compare head to head with Co-LLM, CITER, FusionRoute, Expert Token Routing, contrastive decoding, and simple logit ensembles at matched memory and FLOPs?
Can a sequence-level theorem account for the different prefix distributions induced by specialist, generalist, and routed policies?
Which alternative signals—mutual calibration, entropy-conditioned JS, verifier scores, or semantic disagreement—better distinguish harmful from harmless divergence?
Would allowing multi-token generalist spans, gradual return of control, or bidirectional routing outperform one-token fallback?
How much of the reported gain survives repeated stochastic samples, exact-match constrained decoding, and confidence intervals?
Can the cross-tokenizer top-k approximation be given error bounds relative to full character- or byte-level divergence?
Does fusion improve factual calibration and scientific validity, not only benchmark answer accuracy?
Can KV-cache sharing, quantization, or heterogeneous serving reduce the two-model memory and latency cost?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to Decode Collaboratively with Multiple Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Co-LLM learns a latent token-level decision for when a generalist should invoke domain experts and reports joint performance above individual models. Divergence Decoding removes all router training and uses symmetric predictive disagreement, trading data-free deployment for a cruder hand-thresholded policy.

competitive_landscape.title: An Expert is Worth One Token: Synergizing Multiple Expert LLMs as Generalist via Expert Token Routing
competitive_landscape.difference: Expert Token Routing trains a meta-LLM to emit expert tokens and can integrate or extend multiple experts. The present method uses only two frozen full models and no training, making it easier to deploy but unable to learn expertise boundaries or choose among many experts.

competitive_landscape.title: CITER: Collaborative Inference for Efficient Large Language Model Decoding with Token-Level Routing
competitive_landscape.difference: CITER trains a policy-optimization router to send critical tokens to a large model while explicitly rewarding quality and inference cost. Divergence Decoding instead routes between specialist expertise and general reasoning from JS alone, requires no router data, and does not directly optimize its latency-quality frontier.

competitive_landscape.title: Token-Level LLM Collaboration via FusionRoute
competitive_landscape.difference: FusionRoute jointly trains expert selection and a complementary logit generator, and its theory argues that pure expert-only routing cannot generally recover the optimal policy without strong global coverage. Divergence Decoding is exactly a pure hard router under strong specialist/generalist coverage assumptions; its distinctive benefit is training-free JS gating, not a richer policy class.

competitive_landscape.title: Contrastive Decoding: Open-ended Text Generation as Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Contrastive Decoding combines expert and amateur logits through a plausibility-constrained difference to suppress shared degeneration, without training. Divergence Decoding uses disagreement only as a hard switch between a domain specialist and generalist, preserving one constituent distribution at each token instead of forming a contrastive objective.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is a general training-free paradigm for token-level capability fusion, with JS disagreement theoretically justifying when a specialist should retain control and when a generalist should intervene; the composed policy can exceed both models. Reviewer inference: token-level multi-LLM collaboration, expert routing, and training-free two-model decoding all have substantial prior art. The defensible novelty is the simple asymmetric JS-gated reinterpretation of block speculative decoding for specialist/generalist scientific pairs, plus its early-token mechanism analysis. The theorem mainly formalizes assumptions under which a perfect disagreement separator must work and does not establish sequence-level superiority. Novelty and evidence should therefore be stated as a low-training-cost routing heuristic with promising benchmark gains, not the first token-level capability fusion framework or a general guarantee of A+B>A,B.
reviewer_notes: Full text, theory proof, implementation details, sensitivity tables, resource table, case studies, and limitations were checked through page 20. The record explicitly distinguishes aggregate gains from task-level regressions and identifies a theoretical gap: the proof uses one common expectation over states even though autoregressive policies induce different state distributions. Primary competitors were independently checked on arXiv: 2403.03870, 2403.16854, 2502.01976, 2601.05106, and 2210.15097.
